gancho: O primeiro cabo telegráfico sob o Atlântico, de 1858, funcionou só três semanas. O eletricista-chefe, um médico sem formação em física, forçou até 2.000 volts por ele e ajudou a arruinar a isolação.
explicacao: Dois homens-chave do projeto não se entendiam. William Thomson calculou que o sinal chegaria lento e borrado num cabo tão longo, por um efeito chamado retardo. Wildman Whitehouse, médico que largara a clínica pela nova eletricidade, sem formação em física, contestou a previsão. Thomson criou o galvanômetro de espelho, sensível o bastante para ler os pulsos fracos, enquanto Whitehouse preferia impor tensões altas para mover os telégrafos impressores comuns. Com o cabo pronto, em agosto de 1858, a mensagem de 98 palavras da rainha Vitória ao presidente Buchanan levou cerca de 16 horas para ser transmitida. Nova York comemorou com salva de 100 tiros e fogos de artifício, que causaram um incêndio na prefeitura. Mas as tentativas de Whitehouse de empurrar até 2.000 volts pelo cabo comprometeram a isolação, e em setembro, depois de 732 mensagens, a linha morreu. Ele foi responsabilizado e demitido, embora haja quem argumente que a fabricação e o manuseio ruins do cabo o fariam falhar de qualquer forma. A ligação permanente só veio em 1866.

fontes.trecho: The cable was destroyed after three weeks when Wildman Whitehouse applied excessive voltage to it while trying to achieve faster operation. It has been argued that the cable's faulty manufacture, storage and handling would have caused its premature failure in any case. [...] The first official telegram to pass between two continents that day was a letter of congratulations from Queen Victoria of the United Kingdom to President of the United States James Buchanan. [...] Test messages were sent from Newfoundland beginning 10 August 1858. [...] a grand salute of 100 guns resounded in New York City, streets were hung with flags, bells of the churches were rung, and at night the city was illuminated. On 1 September there was a parade, followed by an evening torchlight procession and a fireworks display that caused a fire in the Town Hall. [...] Whitehouse was a medical doctor by training, but had taken an enthusiastic interest in the new electrical technology and given up his medical practice to follow a new career. He had no formal training in physics; all his knowledge was gained through practical experience. [...] Whitehouse disputed Thomson's law of squares when the latter presented it to a British Association meeting in 1855. Thomson's law predicted that transmission speed on the cable would be very slow due to an effect called retardation. [...] he developed his mirror galvanometer, an extremely sensitive instrument, much better than any until then. [...] driving it with a massive high-voltage induction coil producing several thousand volts, so enough current would be available to drive standard electromechanical printing telegraphs used on inland telegraphs. [...] Whitehouse's repeated attempts to drive up to 2,000 volts through the cable, compromised the cable's insulation. [...] Whitehouse was held responsible for the failure and dismissed. [...] A total of 732 messages were passed before the cable failed. [...] In September 1858, after several days of progressive deterioration of the insulation, the cable failed altogether. [...] Queen Victoria's message of 98 words took 16 hours to send. [...] Since 1866, there has been a permanent cable connection between the continents.

gancho: Em 1834, dois banqueiros franceses subornaram operadores do telégrafo óptico do governo para mandar a Bordeaux a tendência da bolsa de Paris, escondida em erros de propósito nas mensagens oficiais.
explicacao: A França tinha uma rede de torres com braços articulados, o sistema Chappe, que repassavam sinais de torre em torre. A rede era reservada ao governo. Os irmãos François e Joseph Blanc perceberam que, se soubessem antes se a bolsa de Paris subia ou caía, poderiam lucrar em Bordeaux, que seguia Paris com dias de atraso, quando as notícias chegavam pelos jornais. Pôr uma mensagem própria na linha seria descoberto. A saída foi combinar erros deliberados, inseridos em mensagens legítimas e visíveis a um cúmplice que observava as torres perto de Bordeaux. O ponto escolhido foi uma estação perto de Tours, porque ali um inspetor que conhecia o código secreto limpava os erros das mensagens: erros inseridos antes de Tours seriam apagados. Para não deixar nada escrito, os operadores subornados sabiam a direção do mercado pela cor do embrulho de um pacote enviado pela diligência, branco ou cinza; outra versão diz que a mulher do operador recebia meias quando o mercado caía e luvas quando subia. O esquema funcionou por dois anos, até ser descoberto em 1836. Em 1844, Alexandre Dumas pôs no Conde de Monte Cristo um golpe parecido: o conde suborna um operador para transmitir uma notícia falsa e derrubar um rival na bolsa.

fontes.trecho: The network was reserved for government use, but an early case of wire fraud occurred in 1834 when two bankers, François and Joseph Blanc, bribed the operators at a station near Tours on the line between Paris and Bordeaux to pass Paris stock exchange information to an accomplice in Bordeaux. [...] An accomplice at Paris would know whether the market was going up or down days before the information arrived in Bordeaux via the newspapers, after which Bordeaux was sure to follow. The message could not be inserted in the telegraph directly because it would have been detected. Instead, pre-arranged deliberate errors were introduced into existing messages which were visible to an observer at Bordeaux. Tours was chosen because it was a division station where messages were purged of errors by an inspector who was privy to the secret code used and unknown to the ordinary operators. The scheme would not work if the errors were inserted prior to Tours. The operators were told whether the market was going up or down by the colour of packages (either white or grey paper wrapping) sent by mail coach, or, according to another anecdote, if the wife of the Tours operator received a package of socks (down) or gloves (up) thus avoiding any evidence of misdeed being put in writing. The scheme operated for two years until it was discovered in 1836. [...] In Chapter 60 ("The Telegraph") of Alexandre Dumas' The Count of Monte Cristo (1844), the title character describes with fascination the semaphore line's moving arms [...] He later bribes a semaphore operator to relay a false message in order to manipulate the French financial market.

gancho: Minutos antes de o Titanic bater no iceberg, o único operador de rádio do Californian, parado no gelo ali perto, desligou o aparelho e foi dormir. Após o naufrágio, a escuta contínua virou regra em navios de passageiros.
explicacao: Na noite de 14 de abril de 1912, o Californian estava parado, cercado de gelo. O comandante pediu ao operador, Cyril Evans, que avisasse o Titanic, o único navio que ele sabia estar por perto. Como os dois navios estavam relativamente próximos, o aviso chegou fortíssimo e abafou o que Jack Phillips, no Titanic, recebia da estação de Cape Race, na Terra Nova, a uns 1.300 km: ele estava ocupado despachando um acúmulo de mensagens de passageiros. Phillips respondeu com o jargão seco dos operadores: "Saia; estou falando com Cape Race". Ao contrário do que muitos contam, Evans não se ofendeu. Ficou escutando mais um pouco, desligou o equipamento e foi dormir. Às 23h40, o Titanic bateu no iceberg, e logo depois da meia-noite mandou o primeiro pedido de socorro. No Californian, um oficial chegou a ver luzes de outro barco e a tentar contato por lanterna de sinais, sem resposta. Só de manhã, quando acordaram Evans, souberam do naufrágio. Depois do desastre, uma emenda de julho de 1912 a uma lei americana de 1910 passou a exigir dois ou mais operadores e escuta contínua nos navios de passageiros, e a primeira Convenção Internacional para a Salvaguarda da Vida Humana no Mar também previu escuta de rádio 24 horas.

fontes.trecho: On Sunday 14 April at 18:30 ship's time, Californian's only Wireless operator, Cyril Furmstone Evans, signalled to the Antillian [...] Lord asked Evans if he knew of any ships in the area, and Evans responded: "only the Titanic." Lord asked Evans to inform her that Californian was stopped and surrounded by ice. [...] At the time Titanic's on-duty wireless operator, Jack Phillips, was busy clearing a backlog of passengers' messages with the wireless station at Cape Race, Newfoundland, 800 miles (1,300 km) away. Evans's message that Californian was stopped and surrounded by ice was heard very strongly on Titanic due to the relative proximity of the two ships and drowned out a separate message Phillips had been in the process of receiving from Cape Race, prompting Phillips to tell Evans to stop transmitting in the straight diction of wireless operators: "Keep out; I am working Cape Race." [...] Contrary to common belief, Evans was not offended nor did he take the common code for "stop transmitting" to be an insult. Instead, he listened in for a while before he switched off his wireless equipment and went to bed. A few minutes later, at 23:40, Titanic hit an iceberg. Shortly after midnight, she transmitted her first distress call. [...] he had seen the lights of another ship come into view [...] The latter suggested that the ship be contacted by Morse lamp, which was tried, but no reply was seen. [...] He sent Stewart to wake Evans and find out what happened to the ship they had seen to the south. They subsequently learned from the Frankfurt that the Titanic had sunk overnight. [...] The first International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea formed a treaty that also required 24-hour radio monitoring

The new law required that all passenger-carrying ocean vessels of any nationality leaving a U.S. port had to be fitted with efficient radio apparatus when carrying 50 or more passengers and crew. [...] It was approved on June 24, 1910 as Public Law No. 262 [...] In response to the sinking of the RMS Titanic in April 1912, some of the provisions of the original act were strengthened by an amendment passed on July 23, 1912. [...] and a requirement that ships carry two or more operators and maintain a continuous watch.

gancho: Em 1912, uma lei dos EUA confinou a maioria dos radioamadores a ondas mais curtas que 200 metros, então tidas como inúteis para longa distância. Nos anos 1920, eles mostraram que essas ondas curtas cruzavam oceanos.
explicacao: No começo do rádio, falar longe exigia ondas longas, com transmissores caríssimos e antenas gigantes. Nos EUA, a Lei do Rádio de 1912, assinada meses depois do naufrágio do Titanic, passou a exigir licenças e limitou a maioria das estações amadoras a comprimentos de onda abaixo de 200 metros. Isso reduziu muito o alcance delas, e a regra ecoava o que se pensava em vários países: as frequências acima de 1,5 MHz eram vistas como imprestáveis para longa distância e, em muitos países, estavam reservadas aos amadores. Eles insistiram. Em dezembro de 1921, radioamadores podem ter feito os primeiros testes transatlânticos bem-sucedidos, ainda perto dos 200 metros. Com as novas válvulas eletrônicas, os amadores desceram cada vez mais. Em 1923, alguns, com licença especial para ir abaixo dos 150 metros, fizeram nos 100 metros os primeiros contatos de ida e volta pelo Atlântico, e em 1924 muitos já faziam contatos de rotina a 9.600 km ou mais; amadores da Califórnia chegaram a trocar mensagens com um da Nova Zelândia. Ao mesmo tempo, a equipe de Marconi também testava ondas curtas. Hoje elas levam rádio internacional a continentes inteiros.

fontes.trecho: is a United States federal law which was the country's first legislation to require licenses for radio stations. [...] The issue gained importance twelve days later due to the sinking of the Titanic [...] The resulting Radio Act of 1912 was signed by President Taft on August 13, 1912 [...] A key provision was the restriction of most amateur stations to wavelengths below 200 meters (frequencies above 1500 kHz), an assignment that greatly limited their transmitting range until the discovery a decade later of the great distances achievable through shortwave transmissions.

Shortwave radio is used for broadcasting of voice and music to shortwave listeners over very large areas; sometimes entire continents or beyond. [...] the very expensive transmitters, receivers and gigantic antennas. [...] Prior to the 1920s, the shortwave frequencies above 1.5 MHz were regarded as useless for long-distance communication and were designated in many countries for amateur use. Guglielmo Marconi, pioneer of radio, commissioned his assistant Charles Samuel Franklin to carry out a large-scale study into the transmission characteristics of short-wavelength waves [...] Radio amateurs may have conducted the first successful transatlantic tests in December 1921, operating in the 200 meter mediumwave band [...] Although operation on wavelengths shorter than 200 meters was technically illegal (but tolerated at the time as the authorities mistakenly believed that such frequencies were useless for commercial or military use), amateurs began to experiment with those wavelengths using newly available vacuum tubes shortly after World War I. [...] forced amateurs to shift to shorter and shorter wavelengths. [...] A few fortunate amateurs who obtained special permission for experimental communications at wavelengths shorter than 150 meters completed hundreds of long-distance two-way contacts on 100 meters (3 MHz) in 1923 including the first transatlantic two-way contacts. By 1924 many additional specially licensed amateurs were routinely making transoceanic contacts at distances of 6,000 miles (9,600 km) and more. On 21 September 1924 several amateurs in California completed two-way contacts with an amateur in New Zealand.

gancho: Em 1901, Marconi anunciou ter ouvido do outro lado do Atlântico a letra S em código Morse. Até hoje há dúvidas: ninguém confirmou de forma independente, e o teste foi de dia, a pior hora para aquela onda.
explicacao: O sinal teria saído da estação de Poldhu, na Cornualha, e chegado a Signal Hill, na Terra Nova, a cerca de 3.500 km, em 12 de dezembro de 1901, captado com uma antena de 150 m presa a uma pipa. Muitos celebraram o feito como um marco da ciência, mas as dúvidas surgiram logo e nunca se dissiparam. A onda usada estaria perto dos 350 metros, e o teste foi feito numa hora em que todo o caminho sobre o oceano estava sob a luz do dia. Marconi ignorava, mas não havia momento pior: nesse comprimento de onda, a ionosfera diurna absorve o sinal com força e impede o alcance longo. Além disso, não foi um teste às cegas: Marconi sabia que devia esperar três cliques repetidos, a letra S. Os cliques foram ouvidos fracos e esporádicos, difíceis de separar do ruído atmosférico. Desafiado, ele fez em 1902 um teste mais bem documentado, a bordo do navio Philadelphia. Captou sinais registrados em fita a até 2.490 km e ouvidos a até 3.400 km, mas só à noite. De dia, o alcance não passou de uns 1.100 km, menos da metade da distância de Signal Hill. Esse teste foi o primeiro a mostrar que ondas médias e longas vão muito mais longe à noite.

fontes.trecho: the message was received at Signal Hill in St. John's, Newfoundland (now part of Canada), on 12 December 1901, using a 500-foot (150 m) kite-supported antenna for reception – signals transmitted by the company's new high-power station at Poldhu, Cornwall. The distance between the two points was about 2,200 miles (3,500 km). It was heralded as a great scientific advance, yet there also was – and continues to be – considerable scepticism about this claim. The exact wavelength used is not known, but it is fairly reliably determined to have been in the neighbourhood of 350 metres [...] The tests took place at a time of day during which the entire transatlantic path was in daylight. It is now known (although Marconi did not know then) that this was the worst possible choice. At this medium wavelength, long-distance transmission in the daytime is not possible because of the heavy absorption of the skywave in the ionosphere. It was not a blind test; Marconi knew in advance to listen for a repetitive signal of three clicks, signifying the Morse code letter S. The clicks were reported to have been heard faintly and sporadically. There was no independent confirmation of the reported reception, and the transmissions were difficult to distinguish from atmospheric noise. [...] Feeling challenged by sceptics, Marconi prepared a better-organised and documented test. In February 1902, the SS Philadelphia sailed west from Great Britain with Marconi aboard, carefully recording signals sent daily from the Poldhu station. The test results produced coherer-tape reception up to 1,550 miles (2,490 km), and audio reception up to 2,100 miles (3,400 km). The maximum distances were achieved at night, and these tests were the first to show that radio signals for medium wave and longwave transmissions travel much farther at night than during the day. During the daytime, signals had been received up to only about 700 miles (1,100 km), less than half of the distance claimed earlier at Newfoundland

gancho: Em 1880, Graham Bell transmitiu a voz sem fio, num feixe de luz do sol, a cerca de 213 metros. Ele dizia que o fotofone era sua maior invenção, maior que o telefone, e quis dar esse nome à filha.
explicacao: A ideia veio de uma propriedade recém-descoberta do selênio: sua resistência elétrica muda com a luz. Num artigo de 1878, o pesquisador Robert Sabine só via esse efeito num medidor. Bell raciocinou que, pondo um fone no mesmo circuito, poderia ouvir o que Sabine apenas via. No transmissor, a voz fazia vibrar um espelho fino, que ficava ora côncavo, ora convexo, e assim espalhava ou concentrava a luz do sol refletida. No receptor, um espelho parabólico concentrava o feixe numa célula de selênio ligada a um fone, e a luz variável virava som. No primeiro sucesso, Bell ouviu o assistente Charles Sumner Tainter cantando "Auld Lang Syne". Depois, Tainter falou do telhado de uma escola para o laboratório, a cerca de 213 metros, e Bell respondeu acenando com o chapéu da janela. Bell tinha 18 patentes só em seu nome e 12 em parceria; quatro eram do fotofone. Pouco antes de morrer, disse a um repórter que aquela era sua maior invenção, maior que o telefone. Queria batizar a segunda filha de "Photophone", mas a mulher, Mabel, o dissuadiu, e a menina virou Marian. O aparelho é considerado precursor da comunicação por fibra óptica, que se popularizou a partir dos anos 1980.

fontes.trecho: The photophone is a telecommunications device that allows transmission of speech on a beam of light. It was invented jointly by Alexander Graham Bell and his assistant Charles Sumner Tainter on February 19, 1880 [...] Bell's assistant transmitted a wireless voice telephone message from the roof of the Franklin School to the window of Bell's laboratory, some 213 meters (about 700 ft.) away. Bell believed the photophone was his most important invention. Of the 18 patents granted in Bell's name alone, and the 12 he shared with his collaborators, four were for the photophone, which Bell referred to as his "greatest achievement", telling a reporter shortly before his death that the photophone was "the greatest invention [I have] ever made, greater than the telephone". The photophone was a precursor to the fiber-optic communication systems that achieved worldwide popular usage starting in the 1980s. [...] Under the action of the voice the mirror becomes alternately convex and concave and thus alternately scatters and condenses the light. [...] In its ultimate electronic form, the photophone receiver used a photoresistor based on a selenium cell at the focus of a parabolic mirror. [...] Bell likely read of the newly discovered property of selenium having a variable resistance when acted upon by light, in a paper by Robert Sabine as published in Nature on 25 April 1878. In his experiments, Sabine used a meter to see the effects of light acting on selenium connected in a circuit to a battery. However Bell reasoned that by adding a telephone receiver to the same circuit he would be able to hear what Sabine could only see. [...] When the modulated light beam fell upon their selenium receiver Bell, on his headphones, was able to clearly hear Tainter singing Auld Lang Syne. [...] using plain sunlight as their light source [...] Tainter, who was on the roof of the Franklin School, spoke to Bell, who was in his laboratory listening and who signaled back to Tainter by waving his hat vigorously from the window, as had been requested. [...] he wanted to name his new second daughter "Photophone", which was subtly discouraged by his wife Mabel Bell (they instead chose "Marian"

gancho: Na véspera do lançamento do Telstar 1, que levaria imagens de TV ao vivo dos EUA à Europa em 1962, os EUA explodiram uma bomba termonuclear no espaço. A radiação deixada por ela fez o satélite falhar meses depois.
explicacao: O teste Starfish Prime explodiu em 9 de julho de 1962, a 400 km de altitude, sobre o Pacífico, com 1,4 megaton. O Telstar 1, uma esfera de 88 cm e 77 kg coberta por 3.600 células solares, subiu no dia seguinte. Treze dias depois, fez a primeira transmissão ao vivo de um programa de TV entre os EUA e a Europa, mesmo com um transmissor de só 14 watts, o que exigia antenas enormes em terra. Mas a explosão tinha criado cinturões artificiais de radiação, que nos meses seguintes danificaram painéis solares e eletrônica de seis ou mais satélites, entre eles o Telstar e o primeiro satélite britânico, o Ariel 1. A partir de novembro, o canal de comando do Telstar passou a falhar; o satélite foi reativado em dezembro, mas o transmissor parou de vez em 21 de fevereiro de 1963. Ele segue em órbita, mudo. A bomba também mostrou seus efeitos em terra: o pulso eletromagnético atingiu o Havaí, a cerca de 1.450 km, apagou uns 300 postes de luz, disparou alarmes e danificou um link de micro-ondas da companhia telefônica, cortando as ligações entre a ilha de Kauai e as outras ilhas.

fontes.trecho: Telstar 1 is a defunct communications satellite launched by NASA on July 10th, 1962. [...] achieving live transmission of broadcast television images between the United States and Europe. Telstar 1 remained active for only 7 months before it prematurely failed due to Starfish Prime, a high-altitude nuclear test conducted by the United States. Although the satellite is no longer operational, it remains in Earth orbit. [...] Spherical in shape, the satellite had a diameter of 88 centimetres (35 in) and weighed 77 kilograms (170 lb). [...] Since the transmitter was very weak, with a radiated power of only 14 watts, and the antenna array was omnidirectional, very large aperture antennas were required at the ground stations to communicate with it. [...] Telstar 1 operated normally from launch until November 1962 when the radiation from the Starfish Prime high altitude nuclear test detonation affected the command channel, which began to behave erratically. [...] On December 20th, the satellite was successfully reactivated, and intermittent data were obtained until February 21st, 1963, when the transmitter failed. The energy used by it was produced by 3,600 solar cells. [...] Thirteen days after the launch, the first live broadcast of a television show between the United States and Europe took place.

It was launched from Johnston Atoll on July 9, 1962, and was the largest nuclear test conducted in outer space [...] A Thor rocket carrying a W49 thermonuclear warhead [...] was launched from Johnston Atoll in the Pacific Ocean [...] The explosion took place at an altitude of 250 miles (400 km) [...] It had a yield of 1.4 Mt [...] causing electrical damage in Hawaii, about 900 miles (1,450 km) away from the detonation point, knocking out about 300 streetlights, setting off numerous burglar alarms, and damaging a telephone company microwave link. The EMP damage to the microwave link shut down telephone calls from Kauai to the other Hawaiian Islands. [...] In the months that followed, these man-made radiation belts eventually caused six or more satellites to fail, as radiation damaged their solar arrays or electronics, including the first commercial relay communication satellite, Telstar 1, as well as the United Kingdom's first satellite, Ariel 1.

gancho: Tubarões mordendo cabos de internet viraram notícia, mas, pelos dados de um comitê do setor, mordidas de peixes não causaram nenhuma falha de cabo entre 2007 e 2014. Os vilões são redes de pesca e âncoras.
explicacao: Quase todo o tráfego de dados que cruza os oceanos passa por cabos no fundo do mar: cerca de 99%, incluindo internet, comunicações militares e transações financeiras. Segundo números da agência reguladora americana, satélites respondem por só 0,37% da capacidade internacional dos EUA. No mar aberto, um cabo costuma ter a grossura de uma mangueira de jardim, e as fibras que levam a luz têm mais ou menos o diâmetro de um fio de cabelo. Perto da costa, ficam enterrados; no fundo do oceano, repousam direto no leito. Falhas são comuns: cerca de 200 por ano, segundo o Comitê Internacional de Proteção de Cabos. Dois terços delas vêm de acidentes com barcos de pesca e navios arrastando âncoras. Tubarões já morderam alguns cabos, e há registros de ataques de peixes-serra; em 1873, uma baleia danificou um cabo no golfo Pérsico, aparentemente tentando usá-lo para raspar cracas. Mas a categoria "mordida de peixe", que inclui tubarões, não causou nenhuma falha entre 2007 e 2014. Quase ninguém percebe as quebras porque as empresas espalham seu tráfego por vários cabos: se um parte, os outros seguram enquanto ele é consertado.

fontes.trecho: For most of its journey across the ocean, a cable is typically as wide as a garden hose. The filaments that carry light signals are extremely thin — roughly the diameter of a human hair. [...] Nearer to the shore cables are buried under the seabed for protection, which explains why you don’t see cables when you go to the beach, but in the deep sea they are laid directly on the ocean floor. [...] Statistics released by U.S. Federal Communications Commission indicate that satellites account for just 0.37% of all U.S. international capacity. [...] Yes! Cable faults are common. On average, there are roughly 200 faults each year, according to data from the International Cable Protection Committee. You rarely hear about these cable faults because most companies that use cables follow a “safety in numbers” approach to usage, spreading their networks' capacity across multiple cables so that if one breaks, their network will continue to run smoothly over the other cables while service is restored on the damaged one. Accidents like fishing vessels and ships dragging anchors account for two-thirds of all cable faults. [...] This is likely one of the most prevalent myths cited in the press. While it’s true that sharks have bitten a few cables in the past, they are not a significant threat. According to data from the International Submarine Cable Protection Committee, fish bites (a category that includes sharks) accounted for zero cable faults between 2007 and 2014.

Cases of sharks biting cables and attacks by sawfish have been recorded. In one case in 1873, a whale damaged the Persian Gulf Cable between Karachi and Gwadar. The whale was apparently attempting to use the cable to clean off barnacles [...] carrying 99% of the data traffic across the oceans. This data includes all internet traffic, military transmissions, and financial transactions.

gancho: As primeiras letras que passaram com sucesso pela ARPANET, rede precursora da internet, foram "lo". Em 1969, um estudante tentou digitar "login", mas o computador do outro lado travou após dois caracteres.
explicacao: A ARPANET foi criada pela agência de pesquisa do Departamento de Defesa dos EUA. O projeto começou em 1966, com a ideia de permitir que computadores distantes compartilhassem recursos, e usava a comutação de pacotes, que, junto com o TCP/IP adotado depois, virou a base técnica da internet. Na noite de 29 de outubro de 1969, o estudante e programador Charley Kline, na Universidade da Califórnia em Los Angeles, tentou se conectar ao computador do Instituto de Pesquisa de Stanford, onde o programador Bill Duvall o acompanhava. Kline digitou o comando "login", e a máquina de Stanford travou depois das duas primeiras letras. Cerca de uma hora depois, com parâmetros ajustados por Duvall, ele tentou de novo e conseguiu entrar. Assim, a primeira transmissão bem-sucedida da rede foram os dois caracteres "lo". O primeiro link permanente entre as duas instituições foi estabelecido em 21 de novembro daquele ano, e a rede só foi declarada operacional em 1971.

fontes.trecho: was the first wide-area packet-switched network with distributed control and one of the first computer networks to implement the TCP/IP protocol suite. Both technologies became the technical foundation of the Internet. The ARPANET was established by the Advanced Research Projects Agency (now DARPA) of the United States Department of Defense. Building on the ideas of J. C. R. Licklider, Bob Taylor initiated the ARPANET project in 1966 to enable resource sharing between remote computers. [...] The network was declared operational in 1971. [...] The first successful host-to-host connection on the ARPANET was made between Stanford Research Institute (SRI) and UCLA, by SRI programmer Bill Duvall and UCLA student programmer Charley Kline, at 10:30 pm PST on 29 October 1969 [...] Kline typed the command "login," but initially the SDS 940 crashed after he typed two characters. About an hour later, after Duvall adjusted parameters on the machine, Kline tried again and successfully logged in. Hence, the first two characters successfully transmitted over the ARPANET were "lo". The first permanent ARPANET link was established on 21 November 1969, between the IMP at UCLA and the IMP at the Stanfo

gancho: Em 1942, a atriz Hedy Lamarr e um compositor patentearam um sistema antibloqueio para guiar torpedos por rádio, inspirado em pianolas. A Marinha dos EUA recusou, e sugeriram que ela vendesse bônus de guerra.
explicacao: Antes de Hollywood, Lamarr acompanhava o primeiro marido, o vendedor de armas Fritz Mandl, em negociações e ouviu ali que as marinhas queriam guiar torpedos. O controle por rádio tinha um problema: o inimigo podia bloquear o sinal. A ideia dela foi o salto de frequência, trocar de canal o tempo todo. O compositor George Antheil entrou com a experiência de uma obra de vanguarda em que tentara sincronizar várias pianolas com rolos iguais. Os dois perceberam que o mesmo tipo de mecanismo, miniaturizado, poderia fazer transmissor e receptor saltarem juntos de frequência. A patente saiu em agosto de 1942, no nome de casada dela, Hedy Kiesler Markey. A Marinha rejeitou o sistema, alegando que seria grande demais para um torpedo, e os dois desistiram. Algo parecido só entrou em uso em 1962, três anos depois de a patente expirar. Vale um cuidado: Lamarr não inventou o salto de frequência, que já existia, nem o Wi-Fi. Mas o espalhamento espectral, do qual a ideia faz parte, está por trás do Bluetooth e das primeiras versões do Wi-Fi. O reconhecimento veio tarde: um prêmio pioneiro em 1997 e o Hall da Fama dos Inventores dos EUA em 2014, após sua morte.

fontes.trecho: At the beginning of World War II, along with composer George Antheil, Lamarr co-invented a radio guidance system for Allied torpedoes that used spread spectrum and frequency hopping technology to defeat the threat of radio jamming by the Axis powers. [...] Similar technology was used in operational systems only beginning in 1962, which was well after World War II and three years after the expiry of the Lamarr–Antheil patent. Frequency hopping, which existed and was utilized before the Lamarr–Antheil patent, is a foundational technology for spread-spectrum communications. Its principles are utilized for secure wireless networking, including Bluetooth and early versions of Wi-Fi, which use variants of spread spectrum to protect data from interception and interference. [...] During the late 1930s, Lamarr attended arms deals with her then-husband, arms dealer Fritz Mandl, "possibly to improve his chances of making a sale". From the meetings, she learned that navies needed "a way to guide a torpedo as it raced through the water." Radio control had been proposed. However, an enemy might be able to jam such a torpedo's guidance system and set it off course. [...] her idea to prevent jamming by frequency hopping met Antheil's previous work in music. In that earlier work, Antheil attempted synchronizing note-hopping in the avant-garde piece written as a score for the film Ballet Mécanique (1923–24) that involved multiple synchronized player pianos. [...] Together, they realized that radio frequencies could be changed similarly, using the same kind of mechanism, but miniaturized. [...] granted as U.S. patent 2,292,387 on August 11, 1942, under her legal name Hedy Kiesler Markey. The invention was proposed to the Navy, who rejected it on the basis that it would be too large to fit in a torpedo, and Lamarr and Antheil, shunned by the Navy, pursued their invention no further. It was suggested that Lamarr invest her time and attention to selling war bonds since she was a celebrity. [...] Jointly honored with George Antheil with the Electronic Frontier Foundation's Pioneer Award for their work on spread-spectrum technology (1997). [...] Posthumously inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame for her role in the development of frequency-hopping spread spectrum technology (2014).

gancho: Em 2010, uma empresa gastou US$ 300 milhões num cabo de fibra quase reto de Chicago a Nova Jersey para operadores da bolsa ganharem milissegundos. Antenas pelo ar foram mais rápidas: no vidro, a luz é mais lenta.
explicacao: No mercado de alta frequência, operadores lucram com diferenças mínimas de preço entre contratos futuros negociados em Chicago e as ações correspondentes em Nova York. Quem vê a diferença primeiro fecha o negócio antes dos concorrentes. A Spread Networks abriu em 2010 uma linha de 1.331 km entre Chicago e o centro de dados da Nasdaq em Carteret, Nova Jersey, construída em segredo para não ser copiada. A ida e volta do sinal levava cerca de 13 milissegundos, contra uns 14,5 num cabo comum. Só que a luz anda mais devagar no vidro, com índice de refração perto de 1,5, do que no ar, perto de 1. Por isso, na fibra, o tempo de ida e volta é 50% maior que pelo ar. Empresas passaram a transmitir pelo ar, de antena em antena, e chegaram a 8,2 e 8,5 milissegundos, bem perto do mínimo teórico, de cerca de 7,9 a 8. Em 2017, a Spread Networks foi vendida por US$ 127 milhões, menos da metade do que custou o cabo.

fontes.trecho: Its customers are primarily firms engaged in high-frequency trading, where small reductions in latency are important to the extent that they help one close trades before one's competitors. [...] The first cable line, running 827 miles (1,331 km) from Chicago (home to the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, where futures and options are traded) to Carteret, New Jersey (home to the Nasdaq data center), laid at a cost of US$300 million, was unveiled in June 2010. [...] the fund would search out tiny discrepancies between futures contracts in Chicago and their underlying equities in New York. [...] Construction was in full swing (but in extreme secrecy, to avoid getting scooped by competitors) by early 2009. [...] Announced November 27, 2017, Zayo Group Holdings, Inc. ("Zayo") (NYSE: ZAYO) entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Spread Networks for $127 million in cash. [...] Spread Networks uses fiber optic cables along a route as close to straight as possible [...] Their estimated roundtrip time along the dark fiber line (from Chicago to Carteret) is 13 milliseconds. [...] According to a Wired article, the estimated roundtrip time for an ordinary cable is 14.5 milliseconds, giving users of Spread Networks a slight advantage. However, because glass has a higher refractive index than air (about 1.5 compared to about 1), the roundtrip time for fiber optic cable transmission is 50% more than that for transmission through the air. Some companies, such as McKay Brothers, Metrorede and Tradeworx, are using air-based transmission to offer lower estimated roundtrip times (8.2 milliseconds and 8.5 milliseconds respectively) that are very close to the theoretical minimum possible (about 7.9-8 milliseconds).

gancho: Conta-se que a central telefônica automática nasceu da desconfiança de um agente funerário: Almon Strowger achava que a telefonista, mulher de um concorrente, desviava as ligações dos clientes dele.
explicacao: Nas primeiras centrais, era uma telefonista quem ligava os fios entre quem chamava e quem era chamado. Almon Strowger, veterano da Guerra Civil americana, foi professor no campo e depois virou agente funerário no meio-oeste americano (as fontes citam cidades do Kansas e Kansas City, no Missouri). Pela versão que se repete, ele percebeu que perdia clientes quando leu no jornal que o enterro de um amigo tinha ficado com outra funerária. Desconfiou da telefonista local, casada com um concorrente, e decidiu eliminar o intermediário. Em 1889 inventou uma central automática, patenteada em 1891; diz-se que o primeiro modelo foi montado com uma caixa redonda de colarinhos e alfinetes. A primeira central comercial com o sistema abriu em La Porte, Indiana, em 3 de novembro de 1892, com cerca de 75 assinantes e espaço para 99. Strowger ficou com pouco do valor que a invenção alcançaria: vendeu as patentes aos sócios em 1896 por US$ 1.800 e sua parte na empresa em 1898 por US$ 10 mil. Em 1916, essas patentes foram revendidas ao sistema Bell por US$ 2,5 milhões.

fontes.trecho: In October 1861, he enlisted as a Musician in Company A, 8th New York Cavalry Regiment, to fight in the American Civil War. [...] After the Civil War, it appears he first became a country school teacher before he became an undertaker. He is variously attributed as living in El Dorado, Kansas, or Topeka, Kansas, and finally Kansas City, Missouri. [...] A commonly told story holds that Strowger believed that his undertaking business was losing clients to a competitor whose wife was a local telephone operator and was preventing telephone calls from being routed to Strowger's business and re-routing them to her husband's business instead, following his discovery in the newspaper that a friend's funeral was being handled elsewhere. Motivated to remove the intermediary operator, he invented the first automatic telephone exchange in 1889; he received its patent in 1891. It is reported that he initially constructed a model of his invention from a round collar box and some straight pins. [...] it installed and opened the first commercial exchange in (his then home town of) La Porte, Indiana, on November 3, 1892, with about 75 subscribers and capacity for 99. [...] Strowger sold his patents to his associates in 1896 for $1,800 [...] and sold his share in the Automatic Electric Company for $10,000 [...] in 1898. His patents were subsequently sold to Bell Systems for $2.5 million in 1916

gancho: Graham Bell atendia o telefone com "ahoy, ahoy", saudação de marinheiros, que não pegou. Em 1877, Thomas Edison propôs "hello" numa carta: o grito se ouvia a vários metros e dispensaria uma campainha.
explicacao: O "hello" já aparecia por escrito nos EUA desde 1826. As palavras da família tinham outros usos: "hullo" era uma exclamação de surpresa, usada por Charles Dickens em 1850, e "halloo" era o grito para chamar o barqueiro de uma balsa. Por um relato, "halloo" foi a primeira palavra que Edison gritou no fonógrafo ao descobrir o som gravado, em 1877. Bell, logo depois de inventar o telefone, preferia o "ahoy" dos navios, mas não há indício de que a moda tenha pegado. Em 15 de agosto de 1877, Edison escreveu ao presidente de uma companhia de telégrafo de Pittsburgh que não precisariam de campainha, porque "Hello!" podia ser ouvido a 10 ou 20 pés de distância. Edison é apontado como quem popularizou a saudação. Em 1880, crachás com "Hello" podem ter aparecido na primeira convenção de telefonistas, nas Cataratas do Niágara, e em 1889 as telefonistas das centrais já eram chamadas de "hello-girls".

fontes.trecho: Thomas Edison is credited with popularizing hullo as a telephone greeting. In previous decades, hullo had been used as an exclamation of surprise (used early on by Charles Dickens in 1850) and halloo was shouted at ferry boat operators by people who wanted to catch a ride. According to one account, halloo was the first word Edison yelled into his strip phonograph when he discovered recorded sound in 1877. Shortly after Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone, he answered calls by saying "ahoy ahoy", borrowing the term used on ships. There is no evidence the greeting caught on. Edison suggested Hello! on August 15, 1877, in a letter to the president of Pittsburgh's Central District and Printing Telegraph Company, T. B. A. David: Friend David, I do not think we shall need a call bell as Hello! can be heard 10 to 20 feet away. [...] The first name tags to include Hello may have been in 1880 at Niagara Falls, which was the site of the first telephone operators convention. By 1889, central telephone exchange operators were known as "hello-girls" because of the association between the greeting and the telephone. [...] Hello, with that spelling, was used in publications in the U.S. as early as the 18 January 1826 edition of the Norwich Courier

gancho: SOS não quer dizer "save our souls". O sinal nasceu numa regra alemã de 1905 como uma sequência contínua de três pontos, três traços e três pontos, sem letras. As frases vieram depois, para ajudar a decorar.
explicacao: No começo do rádio, cada empresa tinha seu pedido de socorro. A Marconi determinou em 1904 que suas estações usassem CQD. A Alemanha foi a primeira a adotar o SOS, numa regulamentação que entrou em vigor em 1º de abril de 1905. Em 1906, a primeira Convenção Internacional de Radiotelegrafia, em Berlim, tornou-o padrão mundial a partir de 1908: navios em perigo deveriam repetir, a intervalos curtos, três pontos, três traços e três pontos. Nem a lei alemã nem a regra internacional falavam em letras. Como no Morse três pontos formam o S e três traços o O, "S O S" virou um jeito fácil de lembrar a ordem. Só mais tarde surgiram as frases encaixadas na sigla, como "save our souls" (salvem nossas almas) e "save our ship" (salvem nosso navio). A troca não foi imediata: muitos operadores da Marconi resistiram, e em abril de 1912 os do Titanic ainda alternavam CQD e SOS. Depois disso, o CQD foi sumindo.

fontes.trecho: In International Morse Code, three dots form the letter "S" and three dashes make the letter "O", so "S O S" became a common way to remember the order of the dots and dashes. SOS, when it was first agreed upon by the International Radio Telegraphic Convention in 1906, was merely a distinctive Morse code sequence and was initially not an abbreviation. Later, backronyms were created for it in popular usage, and SOS became associated with mnemonic phrases such as "save our souls" and "save our ship". [...] SOS originated in German government maritime radio regulations adopted effective 1 April 1905. It became a worldwide standard when it was included in the service regulations of the first International Radiotelegraph Convention signed on 3 November 1906, which became effective on 1 July 1908. [...] beginning 1 February 1904 "the call to be given by ships in distress or in any way requiring assistance shall be C.Q.D." [...] Germany was the first country to adopt the SOS distress signal [...] "Ships in distress shall use the following signal: [...] repeated at brief intervals". In both the 1 April 1905 German law and the 1906 international regulations, the distress signal is specified as a continuous Morse code sequence of three dots / three dashes / three dots, with no mention of any alphabetic equivalents. [...] However, there was some resistance among Marconi operators to adopting the new signal, and as late as the April 1912 sinking of the RMS Titanic the ship's Marconi operators intermixed CQD and SOS distress calls. In the interests of consistency and maritime safety, the use of CQD appears to have died out thereafter.

gancho: Antes dos satélites de comunicação, a Marinha dos EUA usou a Lua como satélite, refletindo nela sinais de rádio entre Washington e o Havaí. A ideia veio de uma tentativa de espionar radares soviéticos na Lua.
explicacao: Para falar além da curvatura da Terra, o rádio dependia de ondas refletidas pela ionosfera, que erupções solares e tempestades geomagnéticas às vezes atrapalhavam. Antes dos satélites artificiais, a Lua era o único corpo celeste confiável para refletir sinais entre lados opostos do planeta. Em 1946, o Exército americano detectou ondas de radar que voltavam da Lua. Em 1949, um engenheiro do Laboratório de Pesquisa Naval passou a observar a Lua para tentar interceptar sinais de radares soviéticos que batiam nela e voltavam, num programa que em menos de um ano virou espionagem oficial da Marinha. Ao testar uma nova antena, em 1950, a equipe viu que o eco chegava com qualidade muito maior que a esperada, e a escuta virou um sistema de comunicação. A primeira transmissão de voz por esse satélite natural ocorreu em 24 de julho de 1954. Em 1959, funcionava a ligação lunar entre o Havaí e Washington, inaugurada oficialmente em janeiro de 1960 com uma mensagem do chefe de operações navais. O sistema ficou obsoleto no fim dos anos 1960, com os satélites artificiais, mas o que se aprendeu com ele ajudou a torná-los possíveis.

fontes.trecho: Its objective was to develop a secure and reliable method of Wireless communication by using the Moon as a natural communications satellite [...] Operation Moon Relay was spun off from a classified military espionage program known as Passive Moon Relay (PAMOR), which sought to eavesdrop on Soviet military radar signals reflected from the Moon. [...] The first proof of this concept was the Project Diana program of the U.S. Army Signal Corps in 1946, which detected radar waves bounced off the Moon. [...] long distance wireless communication around the curve of the Earth was conducted by skywave ("skip") transmission, in which radio waves are refracted by the Earth's ionosphere, which was sometimes disrupted by solar flares and geomagnetic storms. Before artificial satellites, the Moon provided the only reliable celestial object from which to reflect radio waves to communicate between points on opposite sides of the Earth. [...] The developments in Moon circuit communications eventually came to the attention of James Trexler, a radio engineer at the Naval Research Laboratory. [...] Trexler developed plans for a system designed to intercept Soviet radar signals by detecting the transmissions that bounced off the Moon. This program, codenamed "Joe," began making regular observations in August 1949. Within a year, "Joe" was made an official Navy intelligence program [...] In September 1950, a new parabolic antenna for the PAMOR project was completed at Stump Neck, Maryland. The first tests of this antenna were impressive; the returning signal was of much higher fidelity than expected. This presented the possibility of using a Moon circuit as a communications circuit. [...] the first satellite transmission of voice occurred on July 24, 1954. [...] The experimental system was transformed into a fully operational lunar relay system linking Hawaii with Washington, DC, which became functional in 1959. The new system was officially inaugurated in January 1960, when Chief of Naval Operations Admiral Arleigh Burke sent a message to Commander, Pacific Fleet Felix Stump using the system. [...] The Moon Relay system became obsolete in the later 1960s as the Navy implemented its artificial satellite communication system. However, the information gleaned from the project in fact made the later artificial system possible.
